beats.text: BegFi is a crypto money-movement platform. One link, any EVM chain, in under a minute.

card.title: BegFi, explained
card.lead: One link. Any chain. Under a minute.
points: The four products
The money engine
The safety controls
And what is not built yet

beats.text: It answers a question that sounds trivial and is not: how does somebody with no wallet, and no patience, receive crypto from a group chat, or send it to one?

BegFi's answer is four products sharing one identity, one dashboard, one leaderboard, and one money engine. You can beg for crypto, pay somebody with a link, run a campaign that pays people for work, or give crypto away. Everything settles on chain, and the numbers are public. This video walks through all of it, including the parts that are unfinished.

card.title: Four products, one engine
points: Beg pages — ask with a link
Pay Links — request a fixed amount
Campaigns — pay for verified work
Drops — fund a pot, first come first paid

beats.text: The oldest product is the beg page, and it is still the simplest money path on the site: a profile at slash your username, with an avatar, a bio, socials, a verified X tick, a QR code and a share card.

Anyone can send the token straight to that wallet. Payment pages and tips are wallet to wallet — BegFi never holds those funds and cannot reverse a transaction. A beg is a request with a goal and a progress bar, and every tip produces a receipt at slash t slash transaction hash: a page you can post that proves money moved.
The feed at slash begs is the public wall of them, and the leaderboard ranks everyone who gives, earns and begs across the whole platform.
Product two is Pay Links: a request with an amount and a note. You create one in the dashboard and get a page like this, a QR code for a phone camera, share text, and its own unfurl card.

A Pay Link is deliberately not money. The row in our database is an ask: no balance, no deposit address, no paid flag. The payer's wallet sends straight to the owner's wallet, which is why there is nothing here to lose or to freeze.

card.title: A request is not a balance
points: The row is an ask — no funds, no address
The payer sends wallet to wallet
Settlement is derived from the chain
A partial payment is recorded, never announced

beats.text: Paid is decided by reading the chain. When the indexer confirms a transfer that covers the ask, the run that recorded it settles the request and rings the owner's notification bell. A partial payment is written down but not announced, because calling it paid would be a guess about what the payer meant.

card.title: Confirmed on chain, then a bell
points: The 15-minute indexer confirms the transfer
The same run settles the request
The settling hash is stored on the row
No second watcher, no render-time guessing

beats.text: Product three is Earn, where campaigns live. A project funds a pool, writes the rules, and pays people for verified work: posting about the project, joining it, referring it. There are individual campaigns, and project campaigns that run a daily budget over a period.

Deposits are credited from confirmed on-chain transfers. Rewards are paid once per UTC day, automatically, with no manual approval in between, and posts are verified against X with a pending queue for the ones that need a human to look.

card.title: Fund a pool, pay for work
points: Deposits credited from confirmed transfers
Daily reward cycles, per UTC day
Automatic payouts — no approval step
Verification against X, with a review queue

beats.text: Every campaign has its own leaderboard, and the site-wide one ranks everyone across all of them. It is the most built-out part of the platform, and the engine it uses is the engine everything else now shares.
Product four is the newest: Drops. A drop is a pot of one token, a fixed prize per claim, and a cap on how many people can take it.

card.title: Drops
points: One pot
One fixed prize
A cap on claimers
Paid in seconds

beats.text: Someone funds the pot, sets the prize, and shares the link. The first people to open it sign in, claim, and each receives that prize in their own wallet within seconds. One prize per wallet, and one per verified X account.
The page shows the pot's arithmetic in full: deposited, paid out, promised, and claimable right now. A claim is paid in full or refused — never partial, and never queued behind an empty pot.

What makes Drops interesting is what it did not build. It reuses the campaign payout engine instead of running a second one: the same distributor wallet, the same ledger table, the same lease that makes a double payment impossible, the same kill switch, the same reconciliation. The only genuinely new pieces are how a pot is credited, and a lease that stops two products paying in the same token.

card.title: Drops runs on the campaign engine
points: Same wallet and key
Same payout ledger, one new column
Same lease atom, gas floor, kill switch
New: intent-matched funding, cross-product token lease

beats.text: So how does the money actually move? There is no escrow contract and no smart-contract custody. Pools are funded to a wallet BegFi controls, and paid out automatically by a single key held by the server: the distributor private key.

card.title: No escrow. One hot wallet.
points: Funders send tokens to the payout wallet
The backend pays out from one EOA
The key is a single server secret
Simple, chain-agnostic — and a real risk

beats.text: That is a deliberate trade, and the risks are written down rather than hidden: no escrow means less code to break, but one leaked key would lose everything at once, and there is no hot-cold split yet.

card.title: One key holds the float
points: No KMS, no rotation plan yet
No hot and cold wallet split yet
Known and tracked, not hidden
Mitigated today by stopping power, not by custody

beats.text: Two independent layers stop a double payment. Money truth: a payout only counts once its transaction is confirmed on chain, and a hash is filed before anyone waits for it. And send truth: an atomic lease, claimed in the database before the send, so two runs that try to pay the same person cannot both win.

card.title: Two layers of truth
points: Money truth — confirmed on chain, then counted
Send truth — an atomic lease written before sending
A stale lease expires after ten minutes
A failed send releases it for the next run

beats.text: Everything that leaves the wallet is one row in one ledger, shared by BegFi's own reward pool, every campaign, and every drop. Each send reads the wallet's live token balance first and holds a native-gas floor, so a run stops rather than firing transactions it cannot pay for.

card.title: Three pools, one money trail
points: Pool tokens, rewards and drop prizes in one table
Live balance read before every send
A native-gas floor blocks the run, not the transaction
One audit trail the admin console can read

beats.text: Then there is attribution, which is harder than it sounds when every pool shares one address. A campaign is credited by token alone. A drop is credited by intent: the funder registers which wallet, which pot, and how much, and the scanner credits only transfers that match. A transfer that matches no intent is credited nowhere, on purpose — guessing would credit somebody else's giveaway with your money.

card.title: Credit by intent, not by hope
points: Funder registers wallet, pot and amount
Only matching transfers are credited
An unmatched transfer waits, uncredited
The budget the funder named is the budget we honour

beats.text: Four controls make that engine survivable, and all four exist because a wallet that pays people also has to be able to stop, and to be checked.

card.title: Stop, check, alert, record
points: A kill switch
Hourly reconciliation
Gas alerting
An audit log

beats.text: One: a global kill switch. It is a single row, read at the top of every payout path, and flipped from the admin console. It fails closed: if that row cannot be read, payouts stop. The moment you need a kill switch is the moment the database is misbehaving.

card.title: The kill switch fails closed
points: One row, read at the top of every money path
Unreadable row = no payouts at all
Pausing asks for a reason, because earners read it
Resuming takes one click

beats.text: Two: hourly reconciliation. Every hour, a job compares what each token is owed against the distributor's live on-chain balance, records a row per token, and pauses payouts before it alerts a human. Stopping the bleeding comes first; the notification is second.

card.title: Owed versus held, every hour
points: One row per token, every hour
Drift pauses payouts, THEN alerts
An unreadable balance is reported as unreadable
Owed means promised — not the day's remaining budget

beats.text: Three: gas alerting. The same job watches the wallet's native balance against the sweep's own floor and rings the bell while it is under — the alert that prevents a silent stall. Four: an audit log. Every switch flip, automatic pause, sweep and reconciliation writes an append-only row, written by the code that did the thing.

card.title: Gas warning, permanent record
points: Low gas alerts at most once an hour
Alerts — it does not pause; sending already stops
Every flip, pause and sweep is written down
The writer never blocks the money path

beats.text: Which brings the most unusual page on the site: slash transparency. It publishes the payout wallet's live balance, what is owed right now, all-time paid, the state of the switch and the reason a human gave for pausing it, the latest reconciliation per token, and the recent audit entries.

It renders bad news as readily as good news — a shortfall, a pause, an unreadable reading. That is the point. A transparency page that only looks good when things are good is a marketing page with a ledger in it.

card.title: Publish the ugly truth too
points: Live balance and gas on hand
Owed right now, per token
Switch state and the reason for it
The last actions, in short

beats.text: Now the honest list, because every product video skips this part. Custody first: every pool still funds one shared address, so there are no per-pool deposit addresses, and there is no automatic refund for an unspent pot. The remainder stays in the payout wallet, and the site says so out loud instead of implying a refund that does not exist.

card.title: Custody, addresses, refunds
points: One shared deposit address for every pool
No per-pool attribution by address yet
No automatic refund for an unspent pot
The site says this plainly before you fund

beats.text: Second, sybil resistance. A giveaway or a campaign can be farmed by wallets that are one person without a verified X account. There is no captcha, no clustering by funding source, and no review queue yet. Device fingerprinting existed and was removed on purpose, because it punished shared phones and told honest people to come back tomorrow.

card.title: Sybil resistance is identity only
points: One prize per wallet and per verified X account
No captcha, no clustering, no review queue
Device limits were removed deliberately
The honest ceiling is what the site can check

beats.text: Third, the clock. The indexer is behind the chain — measured at roughly half a million blocks — so anything that depends on it, pay-link settlement and deposit crediting included, arrives late. A funder can accelerate detection by pressing check, and the fix is scanning more windows per run.

card.title: The indexer is behind the chain
points: Measured ~496,000 blocks behind
Deposits and settlements arrive late
A manual check scans a recent window now
Fix: multi-window scans in one time budget

beats.text: And fourth, breadth. The site runs on one chain, Robinhood Chain, so Ethereum and Base are a phase rather than a patch. There is no public API or embeddable button yet, no PWA, and no Play Store listing. Those are the next platform milestones, not repairs.

card.title: One chain, no API, no store
points: Robinhood Chain only, for now
No public API or embeddable pay button yet
No PWA install, so no Play Store listing
More chains is a phase, not a patch

beats.text: So where does it go next? Per-pool deposit addresses, because one change closes attribution, makes refunds possible, and retires the shared-address assumption for all three funding products at once. Then a sybil pass on the claim and submit paths. Then the platform work: more chains, an admin panel that covers everything, and a public API.

card.title: What changes first
points: Per-pool deposit addresses
Refunds for an unspent pot
A sybil pass on claims and submissions
More chains, a fuller admin panel, an API

beats.text: Everything in this video is live at begfi dot io, including the books. Nothing on the site is fake data: an unconfigured feature says it is unconfigured, and a wallet that is short says it is short. That is the whole idea — money movement that is fast, and honest about the parts it has not finished.
